**In Praise of the Half-Finished**

I have a notebook full of sentences that stop mid-thought. A folder of essays with no endings. A drawer of yarn in colors I no longer remember choosing. For years I treated these as failures—evidence of a scattered mind. Lately I have begun to see them differently: as a museum of my curiosity, a record of the moments when I was alive enough to begin.

There is a particular pressure to finish. Finish the book, the project, the thought, the day. We are graded on completion. But so much of life is not a line with a destination; it is a room with many doors left ajar. The unfinished thing is not always abandoned. Sometimes it is still breathing.

Think of a sketch. A sketch is not a failed painting. It is a faster, more honest way of seeing—a hand trying to keep up with the eye. The lines that don’t meet, the shading that stops abruptly, are not mistakes; they are evidence of attention moving at the speed of thought. A finished painting says, *Here is the world.* A sketch says, *Here is me, looking at the world, right now.*

The same is true of conversations that trail off. The sentence that begins, “I was going to say—” and then doesn’t. The friendship that doesn’t end so much as hibernate. The city you meant to visit. The language you learned for three months and forgot. These are not wasted. They are the hum of a life being lived in many directions at once.

I think we are too quick to call things incomplete. A tree in winter is not an unfinished tree. A song that fades out is not a broken song. A person who is still becoming is not a draft of a person. We are all, in some sense, half-finished—and that is not a flaw but a condition of being alive.

The Japanese concept of *wabi-sabi* finds beauty in impermanence and imperfection. A cracked bowl is repaired with gold, and the crack becomes part of its story. What if we treated our unfinished projects that way? Not as things to be hidden or finished out of guilt, but as golden cracks—proof that we tried, that we reached, that we were curious enough to start.

There is a freedom in leaving something open. It allows the future to enter. A finished thing is sealed; an unfinished thing is still in conversation with the world. It can be picked up years later, or never. It can become something else entirely. The half-written poem may become a letter. The abandoned novel may teach you how to write the next one. The unfinished argument may teach you how to listen.

So I have stopped apologizing for my half-finished things. I let them sit on shelves and in folders, like seeds. Not everything needs to bloom. Not everything needs to be finished to be loved. Sometimes the most honest thing you can say is: *I started. I was here. I was curious.* And then you let the sentence trail off, the way life does.

Maybe that’s enough. Maybe the beauty is in the starting, not the ending.
